title: Medicare Advantage Operational Playbook (CleanClaimRx Operational Playbook Series)
audience: Stated: practice administrators, billing managers and revenue-cycle professionals who manage Medicare Advantage plan relationships. Implied by the workflows: an office-based practice with front-desk staff, referral coordinators, scheduled procedures and a billing team.
summary: Vendor primer arguing that Medicare Advantage must be run as a set of separate commercial payers rather than as traditional Medicare with extra paperwork. Ten sections cover plan economics, a five-step prior-authorization workflow built on a per-plan requirement matrix, HCC risk-adjustment capture with yearly recapture and a fourth-quarter gap audit, MA denial categories with an appeal ladder and peer-to-peer calls, claim checkpoints (authorization number, modifiers, coordination of benefits, timely filing), contract inventory and negotiation levers, thumbnail profiles of five national carriers plus regional plans, compliance warnings, Star/HEDIS measures and annual wellness visits, and a management system (dashboard, coordinator role, annual review). A 90-day assessment plan and four checklists close it. The central method: inventory each plan's rules, name an owner, checkpoint every claim, measure monthly. The frame is office-based and procedure-heavy; it cites no regulations and contains material coding, appeals and regulatory errors.

outline.gist: Disclaimers: educational only, not legal or compliance advice, rules change; plus a second boilerplate paragraph about reviewing AI-generated drafts.

outline.section: Introduction: Medicare Advantage Is Not Medicare - And That Difference Is Costing You
outline.gist: MA covers over half of beneficiaries; each plan is a separate commercial payer; a fact box of enrollment and denial statistics; scope of the playbook.

outline.section: Section 1: The MA Landscape - What Your Practice Is Actually Dealing With
outline.gist: Plan economics (risk-adjusted capitation), authorization burden, risk adjustment as second revenue layer, denial environment, contract complexity, and a comparison table versus traditional Medicare.

outline.section: Section 2: Prior Authorization - Building a System That Works
outline.gist: Five-step workflow (identify requirement, submit early, document, track, verify scope), authorization matrix, retrospective requests, appeals, and a warning about post-payment audits.

outline.section: Section 3: Risk Adjustment Coding - Capturing What You Actually Treat
outline.gist: RAF and HCC basics, code-specificity table, yearly recapture, fourth-quarter problem-list audit, the documentation line between proper and improper coding, clinician education.

outline.section: Section 4: Denial Management in the MA Environment
outline.gist: Four denial categories with responses, a five-level appeal table with deadlines and dollar thresholds, and a peer-to-peer call playbook.

outline.section: Section 5: MA-Specific Billing and Claims Operations
outline.gist: Authorization number on the claim, plan-specific modifier handling, coordination of benefits, timely filing limits, and a checkpoint table by role.

outline.section: Section 6: Contract Strategy for MA Plans
outline.gist: Audit each contract's terms, benchmark rates, weigh value-based offers against capability and risk tolerance, use quality and network adequacy as leverage, negotiate MA separately.
Short generic sketches of UnitedHealthcare, Humana, Anthem/Elevance, Aetna/CVS, Cigna and regional plans; no plan rules, deadlines or contact details.

outline.section: Section 8: Compliance - Where MA Gets Dangerous
outline.gist: False Claims Act exposure from unsupported diagnoses, truthful authorization requests, OIG focus areas, six compliance practices, and a warning about retrospective chart-review programs.

outline.section: Section 9: Quality Measures and Their Revenue Impact
outline.gist: Star ratings and bonus mechanics, a table of seven measures, annual wellness visits as the top quality action, plan care-gap reports reviewed monthly.

outline.section: Section 10: Building Your MA Management System
outline.gist: Eight-metric dashboard with targets, owners and cadences; a dedicated MA coordinator above 200 MA patients; an annual MA business review; product catalog.
Days 1-30 baseline (panel, contracts, denials, authorization audit, coding sample); days 31-60 fix authorization, coding and quality gaps; days 61-90 measure and set cadence.
Four checklists: prior authorization (7 items), risk adjustment coding (6), quality measures (5), compliance (6); all restate earlier sections.

outline.section: Closing: MA Is the Future of Medicare - Operate Accordingly
outline.gist: Restates the thesis that deliberate MA operations beat ad hoc handling; no new content; ends with a product cross-sell.

Pre-submission claim scrubbing for coding edits
Coverage verification (MA versus traditional Medicare) every encounter

processes.name: Prior authorization workflow
steps: Keep one authorization matrix per MA plan: services and code ranges needing approval, lead times, submission channel, required documents, validity period
Check the matrix when the service is scheduled and submit the request then
Build the packet from a service-specific documentation checklist
Log submission date, plan reference, expected and actual response, approval number, approved service, dates and units in the practice-management system
Chase open requests before the service date
Compare the approval with the order (service, dates, units, provider) before the claim goes out
Put a medical-necessity statement in the clinical note
processes.owner_role: Authorization coordinator (single named owner of the matrix); nurse or medical assistant assembles packets; billing specialist verifies scope
processes.cadence: Per order; matrix reviewed quarterly, at each contract renewal and on any plan policy notice

processes.name: MA denial triage by category
steps: Sort each denial: authorization deficiency, medical necessity, coding or billing, eligibility or coverage
Split authorization denials into missing, mismatched, expired or wrong provider
Missing: decide on a retrospective request using claim value, documentation strength, reason for the miss and the plan's track record
Mismatch or expired: ask for substitution or a retroactive extension; wrong provider: correct the rendering provider if possible
Coding denials: fix and resubmit, then correct the upstream process rather than appeal
Eligibility denials: re-verify plan enrollment for the service month and bill the right payer
Trend denial rate by plan and category

processes.name: Medical-necessity appeal and peer-to-peer call
steps: For any medical-necessity denial above a set dollar threshold, request a peer-to-peer call within 24 to 48 hours
Pull the criteria the plan cited and the chart evidence that answers each criterion
Treating physician speaks to the plan medical director using a short case narrative
If not reversed, file a written appeal authored by the ordering clinician that rebuts the stated denial reason point by point
Escalate through the remaining appeal levels for high-value cases, watching each filing deadline
processes.owner_role: Ordering or treating physician; billing manager tracks utilization

processes.name: Chronic-condition coding gap audit (risk adjustment)
steps: List active MA patients (start with a 20 to 30 patient sample having three or more chronic conditions)
Compare each active problem list with diagnosis codes billed in the current calendar year
Record conditions not yet coded this year
Address a gap only at an encounter where the clinician documents monitoring, management or relevance of the condition
Check that conditions already coded are supported by the notes
Feed findings into clinician documentation training and a coding checklist
processes.owner_role: Billing manager with clinicians and coders
processes.cadence: Annually in the fourth quarter per the text (the dashboard says quarterly)

processes.name: MA claim pre-submission checkpoints
steps: Verify plan enrollment and MA-versus-traditional status at every encounter
Confirm the authorization number is on the claim (item 23), matches the plan's record and covers the billed code
Check the plan's modifier policy for flagged code pairs
Confirm order of benefits at claim setup
Track each plan's filing limit in the weekly aged-receivables review
processes.owner_role: Front desk or eligibility staff; billing specialist; billing manager; A/R follow-up staff
processes.cadence: Every encounter and claim; weekly for filing-limit review

processes.name: MA contract inventory, benchmarking and negotiation
steps: Read every MA contract in full
Record rate basis (percent of Medicare, fee schedule or capitation), bonus provisions and measure set, risk-sharing terms, term and renewal dates, termination notice, carve-outs
Compare paid rates on highest-volume codes across plans and against market data
Identify leverage: quality results and network adequacy
Evaluate value-based offers against measured quality performance, population-health capacity and loss tolerance
Negotiate MA as its own package, separate from commercial terms
Have an attorney review value-based or risk terms before signing
processes.cadence: Annually; start benchmarking 12 months before a renewal

processes.name: Annual wellness visit and care-gap closure
steps: List MA patients with no wellness visit in the current calendar year
Prompt scheduling at every encounter and by outreach
Bill the visit under G0438 or G0439 rather than as a routine office visit
Download each major plan's care-gap report monthly
Work the gaps into scheduling and care-management routines
Review measure performance against plan benchmarks quarterly

processes.name: MA operating rhythm: 90-day assessment, dashboard and annual business review
steps: Days 1-30: baseline panel by plan, contract terms, 90-day denial rate, wellness-visit rate, authorization denials and a coding sample
Days 31-60: rebuild the authorization matrix and tracking, set a peer-to-peer protocol, run documentation training, enroll in plan gap programs
Days 61-90: re-measure denials, run the full-panel coding gap analysis, flag contracts renewing within 12 months
Stand up the eight-metric dashboard with an owner and cadence per metric
Report findings to the physician-owner
Hold a yearly review of payer mix, renewals, rates, quality, denials and coding-audit results and decide what to renegotiate or rebuild
processes.owner_role: A committed project owner (5 to 10 hours a week); proposed MA coordinator; physician-owner receives the report
processes.cadence: One-time 90 days, then monthly dashboard and an annual review in the fourth quarter

metrics.name: Authorization denial rate
metrics.definition: Not defined; implied share of MA authorization requests the plan denies

metrics.name: Retro authorization rate
metrics.definition: Not defined; implied share of authorizations requested after the service was delivered

metrics.name: HCC gap closure rate
metrics.definition: Share of active chronic conditions that have been coded on a claim in the current year

metrics.name: MA denial rate
metrics.definition: Not defined; implied share of MA claims denied

metrics.name: Peer-to-peer utilization rate
metrics.definition: Share of medical-necessity denials for which a peer-to-peer call was requested

metrics.name: AWV completion rate
metrics.definition: Share of the MA panel with an annual wellness visit completed in the current calendar year

metrics.name: Care gap closure rate
metrics.definition: Not defined; plan-reported open quality gaps closed

metrics.name: MA rate versus benchmark
metrics.definition: Contracted MA rates on high-volume codes compared with market benchmark

metrics.name: MA denial rate by category, trailing 90 days
metrics.definition: Baseline pulled in week 1 of the 90-day plan, overall and by denial category

metrics.name: Annual revenue impact by authorization denial sub-type
metrics.definition: Estimated yearly dollars lost to missing, mismatched, expired and wrong-provider authorization denials

metrics.name: Chronic-condition coding gap count
metrics.definition: Problem-list conditions not coded on any current-year claim, first in a 20-30 patient sample and then for the full MA panel

metrics.name: Authorization matrix review recency
metrics.definition: Whether the matrix for every MA plan has been reviewed recently

metrics.name: Medication adherence (PDC)
metrics.definition: Proportion of days covered for diabetes, RAS-antagonist and statin medications

metrics.name: Blood pressure control
metrics.definition: Hypertensive patients whose blood pressure is below 140/90

metrics.name: Peer-to-peer reversal rate
metrics.definition: Share of peer-to-peer calls that overturn the denial; reported, not set as a target

metrics.name: Plan Star rating
metrics.definition: CMS 1-to-5 star rating of the plan; plan-level, not practice-level
metrics.target: 4 or 5 stars earns the plan a bonus
metrics.red_flag: 3 or fewer stars said to bring restrictions

metrics.name: MA payer mix
metrics.definition: Share of the practice's MA patients enrolled in each plan

metrics.name: HEDIS measure performance versus plan benchmarks
metrics.definition: Practice results on plan quality measures, reviewed quarterly

metrics.name: Risk adjustment factor (RAF)
metrics.definition: Per-enrollee score that sets the plan's monthly payment
metrics.formula: Sum of the patient's HCC coefficients adjusted for demographics

numeric_claims.claim: More than 33 million people were in MA plans as of 2025, over half of eligible beneficiaries (54%)
MA share projected at about 57% by 2031 and about 63-64% by 2034
MA insurers denied 7.7% of prior authorization requests overall, 4.2% to 12.8% by insurer
94% of physicians said prior authorization had some negative effect on patient care
Revenue lost to MA authorization denials, and a per-patient revenue gap for practices without structured MA operations, are asserted with no figure
Typical lead times: 24 hours for urgent procedures, 3-5 business days routine outpatient, 10-14 business days elective surgery
Retrospective authorization requests are usually due within 30-90 days of the date of service
The most effective authorization appeal is filed within 24-48 hours of the denial by a clinician
HCC diagnoses must be reported at least once each calendar year or they drop out of the risk score
Hypertension (I10) carries HCC weight; R03.0 does not
E11.65 is labeled diabetes with CKD and rated High impact versus Low for E11.9; N18.4 High versus N18.9 Low; I70.213 labeled gangrene and rated High
A one-line chronic-condition status note takes about fifteen seconds
Each appeal level has a 60-day filing window; the plan and the independent reviewer each have 60 days to decide
numeric_claims.source_cited: CMS named generally; no regulation cited

numeric_claims.claim: Minimum amount for an ALJ hearing is $190 and for federal court $1,900 (2025)
Peer-to-peer must usually be requested within 24-72 hours of the denial notice
Peer-to-peer reversal rates run roughly 30-80% depending on specialty and plan
Checking the authorization number takes 90 seconds and prevents a 45-day denial cycle
Traditional Medicare has a one-year filing limit; most MA plans require claims within 90-365 days of service
UnitedHealthcare holds about 29% of national MA enrollment as of 2025; Humana is second
Plans rated 4 or 5 stars get a bonus of 5% of benchmark; plans at 3 or fewer stars face restrictions
Blood-pressure control means below 140/90; breast screening is a mammogram in the prior 2 years for women 50-74; adherence is PDC above 80%
Transitions of care means follow-up within 7 or 30 days after discharge
The wellness visit has no patient copay and usually pays more than a standard visit of equal time
Dashboard targets: authorization denials under 5%, retro authorizations under 2%, MA denials under 6%
Dashboard targets: over 90% of active conditions coded, peer-to-peer on over 80% of medical-necessity denials, wellness visits for over 85% of the MA panel
A dedicated MA coordinator usually pays off once a practice has more than 200 active MA patients
The 90-day plan needs 5-10 hours a week from one owner
Coding review sample: 20-30 complex MA patients with three or more chronic conditions
The authorization matrix should be reviewed at least quarterly (checklist: within the last 90 days)
Star bonuses are worth hundreds of millions of dollars to the largest plans

checkable_claims.claim: Redetermination: the MA plan itself, 60 days to file, plan has 60 days to decide. Reconsideration: Independent Review Entity, 60 days to file after redetermination. ALJ hearing: $190+ claim threshold (2025). Federal Court: $1,900+ threshold (2025).
checkable_claims.section: Section 4: MA Appeal Rights and Timelines (table, page 29)
checkable_claims.why: Level names, filing windows, decision clocks and dollar thresholds drive the appeal calendar. If this ladder is the enrollee and non-contract-provider path and is not open to contracted providers for payment disputes, the practice would file in the wrong forum and miss its contract dispute deadlines.

checkable_claims.claim: Common codes like hypertension (I10) carry HCC weight; elevated blood pressure (R03.0) does not.
checkable_claims.why: If I10 has no payment HCC, the document's first teaching example is false, and staff or AI agents trained on it will misjudge which diagnoses affect risk scores and where audit exposure sits.

checkable_claims.claim: Type 2 diabetes with diabetic chronic kidney disease (E11.65) has a much higher RAF impact than Type 2 diabetes uncomplicated (E11.9).
checkable_claims.section: Section 3: The HCC Framework and specificity table (pages 21-22)
checkable_claims.why: E11.65 is the hyperglycemia code (diabetic CKD is E11.22), and under the current V28 model the diabetes categories appear to share one coefficient. Coding to this advice gains nothing and invites audit findings.

checkable_claims.claim: MA plans ... may approve and pay a claim, then months later audit the medical record and recoup payment if the documentation does not support medical necessity - even if the authorization was obtained prospectively.
checkable_claims.section: Section 2: warning box 'The Authorization Audit Trap' (page 19)
checkable_claims.why: 42 CFR 422.138(c) appears to bar an MA plan from later denying a prior-authorized service for lack of medical necessity except for good cause or fraud. If so, the practice should contest such recoupments, not treat them as normal.

checkable_claims.claim: MA plans deny claims on medical necessity grounds ... using proprietary clinical criteria that may differ from CMS national coverage determinations ... the InterQual criteria, the MCG guidelines, or the plan's own proprietary policy.
checkable_claims.why: Since 2024, 42 CFR 422.101(b)(6) and (c) appear to require plans to follow Medicare coverage rules and allow internal criteria only where Medicare's are not fully established. That is the strongest appeal argument for hospital and nursing-facility care and the document omits it.

checkable_claims.claim: HCC diagnoses must be submitted at least once per calendar year for each patient to be included in that year's risk score calculation ... based on the ICD-10 diagnosis codes submitted on claims from all providers.
checkable_claims.section: Section 3: How Risk Adjustment Works; The Annual Recapture Requirement (pages 20-23)
checkable_claims.why: The whole recapture workflow depends on which encounters count (face-to-face visits with eligible clinician types, with one year's diagnoses setting the next year's payment). A facility-based practice needs to know whether hospital and nursing-facility visits qualify.

checkable_claims.claim: Price transparency MRF data includes MA contracted rates alongside commercial rates.
checkable_claims.why: The Transparency in Coverage rule covers group and individual market plans, not Medicare Advantage. If payer files hold no MA rates, the benchmarking method recommended for physician MA rates does not exist as described.

checkable_claims.claim: HEDIS measures most relevant to physician practices include Transitions of Care (follow-up within 7/30 days post-discharge), Annual Wellness Visit (AWV completed in calendar year) and Medication Adherence (PDC > 80%).
checkable_claims.section: Section 9: HEDIS Measures Most Relevant to Physician Practices (table, pages 52-53)
checkable_claims.why: Care-transition and wellness workflows would be built to the wrong specification if the transitions measure is really notification, discharge information, engagement and medication reconciliation within 30 days, and if the wellness-visit and adherence items are not HEDIS measures at all.

topics: False Claims Act exposure in diagnosis coding
authorization tracking in the practice-management system
payer use of AI in authorization review

adopt.idea: Keep a one-page rule sheet for each MA plan (authorization and referral rules, submission channel, filing limit, dispute deadline, modifier and NP-billing quirks) with a named owner and a last-reviewed date.
adopt.why: Turns scattered knowledge into rules a biller or AI agent can apply as claim edits; most MA rework comes from plan-specific rules nobody wrote down.
adopt.note: For a facility-based practice the content changes: primary-care assignment and referral rules for HMO members seen in facilities, which party holds the stay authorization, coverage of care-management, advance-care-planning and wellness codes, and the dispute path in the contract or provider manual. Build it for the four contracted plans; the document supplies none of the content.

adopt.idea: Re-verify coverage on a schedule instead of assuming continuity: at every admission or new facility episode and at least monthly for the standing census.
adopt.why: Billing traditional Medicare for an MA member, or the wrong plan, is a pure avoidable delay, and MA enrollment is month-specific.
adopt.note: The document says 'every encounter' with a front desk in mind. Nursing-facility residents and dual-eligibles can change plans far more often than once a year, so batch eligibility checks on the census are the practical version.

adopt.idea: Use a fixed MA denial taxonomy (authorization sub-types, medical necessity, coding, eligibility) with one standard response per type, trended by plan.
adopt.why: Lets denial work be routed by rule and shows which plan and which root cause is costing money.
adopt.note: Add categories the document lacks for this practice: referral or primary-care-assignment denials, non-covered or bundled care-management codes, clinician not credentialed, and facility stay not authorized.

adopt.idea: Have the treating clinician own medical-necessity arguments: answer the plan's stated criteria point by point, and use a peer-to-peer call where the plan offers one.
adopt.why: Specific rebuttals beat form letters, and published KFF data (not used by the document) show that most appealed MA authorization denials are overturned.
adopt.note: Most medical-necessity fights for this population concern the hospital or nursing-facility stay and are run by the facility; the physician's part is the call and the documentation. Lead with the Medicare coverage rule the plan must follow, which the document never mentions.

adopt.idea: Write a brief status line for each chronic condition actually assessed at a visit, and track that each active condition is addressed at least once per calendar year.
adopt.why: Supports diagnosis coding, visit leveling and care-management eligibility at once, and is the only defensible form of recapture.
adopt.note: Use the current V28 mapping, not the document's examples. The financial benefit is indirect unless a contract shares risk-adjusted revenue; the same documentation also feeds risk scores used in traditional-Medicare ACO and MIPS cost calculations.

adopt.idea: Run a yearly two-way diagnosis audit on a sample of MA charts: conditions documented but not coded, and conditions coded without support, under a written policy with retained workpapers.
adopt.why: Finds legitimate misses while creating the evidence of good faith that matters under the False Claims Act.
adopt.note: The document mentions checking support only in passing and never says what to do with unsupported codes. Add a correction and payer-notification step, and make it impossible for AI billing agents to add a diagnosis that is not in the signed note.

adopt.idea: Vet any plan or vendor chart-review, gap-form or coding-outreach program before taking part; refuse anything that adds diagnoses from old records without a current-year encounter.
adopt.why: These programs are where provider-side risk-adjustment liability usually starts.
adopt.note: Large MA carriers run exactly these outreach programs. Also check whether the program pays per form or per chart, which raises kickback questions. From payment year 2027 CMS excludes diagnoses from unlinked chart reviews, which will change what plans ask for.

adopt.idea: Abstract every MA contract into a term sheet (rate basis and fee-schedule year, bonus programs, term, renewal and termination notice, dispute and recoupment clauses) and negotiate MA separately from other lines.
adopt.why: A practice cannot detect underpayment or time a renegotiation without knowing its own terms.
adopt.note: Add items the document skips: sequestration pass-through, NP payment percentage, lesser-of-charges language, overpayment look-back, and whether care-management and facility visit codes are carved out. The payer price-transparency benchmarking it suggests does not work for MA rates.

adopt.idea: Maintain a due list of MA patients with no wellness visit this calendar year and review each plan's care-gap report monthly.
adopt.why: Wellness visits are paid work the practice already does, and plan gap reports are the only view of what each plan is measuring.
adopt.note: Confirm each plan's frequency rule and whether it pays the visit in a facility setting. Many long-stay and frail patients are excluded from screening measures, so gap lists need filtering before anyone acts on them.

adopt.idea: Run MA as a managed line of business: a small per-plan scorecard with an owner and cadence per metric, plus an annual MA review that ends in decisions.
adopt.why: Gives the owner-as-CFO a repeatable view of which plans are worth their administrative cost.
adopt.note: Keep the structure and replace the metrics: denial rate by plan, days to pay, paid-versus-contract variance, appeal win rate, credentialing status, share of charges. Drop the unsourced targets and never set a diagnosis-capture quota.

practice_relevance.why: Medicare Advantage is a real but minority share of this practice's charges, concentrated in four plans (UnitedHealthcare, Humana, Capital Health Plan, Florida Blue). The document's most developed material is scheduling-time prior authorization for imaging, procedures and surgery, which a facility-based evaluation-and-management practice with no front desk rarely needs. The contract, denial-taxonomy, coverage-verification, documentation and wellness-visit ideas transfer after correction. Nothing addresses hospital or nursing-facility care under MA, institutional or dual-eligible special-needs plans, HMO primary-care assignment, care-management codes, Florida plans, or billing run by AI agents.
sections_that_do_not_apply: Section 2 steps tied to appointment scheduling, surgical and imaging authorizations, nurse-assembled packets and front-desk roles
Section 5 modifier discussion for procedures (59, X-modifiers, 76, global periods); only modifier 25 is occasionally relevant
Section 5 checkpoint owners (front desk, eligibility staff, billing specialist): no such staff exist
Section 7 profiles of Anthem/Elevance, Aetna/CVS and Cigna; nothing on Capital Health Plan or Florida Blue
Section 9 cancer-screening and several chronic-disease measures for long-stay, frail or advanced-illness patients who are excluded from those measures
Section 10 staffing advice (dedicated MA coordinator above 200 patients)
Value-based and downside-risk contracting guidance: too thin to use and not a near-term fit for a two-clinician practice

accuracy_concerns: ICD-10 examples in the specificity table are wrong, checked against the FY2027 code set: E11.65 is type 2 diabetes with hyperglycemia (diabetic CKD is E11.22); I50.43 is acute on chronic combined systolic and diastolic heart failure (diastolic alone is I50.33); I70.213 is atherosclerosis with intermittent claudication of both legs, not gangrene (gangrene is I70.26x).

Says essential hypertension (I10) carries HCC weight. I10 does not map to a payment category in the CMS-HCC model; only certain hypertensive combination codes (with heart failure or advanced kidney disease) do.

Never mentions the V28 (2024 CMS-HCC) model, the only model used for payment since payment year 2026. Under V28 the diabetes categories share one coefficient and the heart-failure categories shown are constrained to be equal, so the table's Low-to-High and Moderate-to-High examples for diabetes and heart failure no longer describe payment; unspecified peripheral vascular disease (I73.9) and the claudication codes dropped out of the payment model.

Presents acute respiratory failure (J96.00) as a 'higher-specificity' form of COPD. It is a separate acute diagnosis; adding it outside a setting where it was actually treated is a recognized audit target.

States that each diagnosis code maps to an HCC and that the risk score uses codes on claims from all providers for 'that year's' score. Most codes map to nothing; only face-to-face or audio-video encounters with eligible clinician types in eligible settings count; and the model is prospective (this year's diagnoses set next year's payment).

Appeals table is wrong in substance. Level 1 at an MA plan is a reconsideration (redetermination is Original Medicare and Part D terminology); an upheld denial is forwarded to the independent reviewer automatically rather than filed by the party; plan clocks are 72 hours expedited, 30 days standard pre-service and 60 days for payment, not a flat 60; the filing window is now generally treated as 65 days from the notice date.

Presents that CMS ladder as the practice's appeal path. Under 42 CFR Part 422 Subpart M it belongs to enrollees (and physicians acting for them before service) and to non-contract providers who sign a waiver of liability. A contracted provider's payment dispute runs under the contract and provider manual, with plan-specific deadlines the document never mentions.
Dollar thresholds are calendar-2025 values. For 2026 they are $200 (ALJ) and $1,960 (federal court) under the Federal Register notice of December 4, 2025.

The 'authorization audit trap' box tells readers a plan may recoup for medical necessity after approving prior authorization. 42 CFR 422.138(c), in force since 2024 and amended in 2025, bars a plan from later denying a prior-authorized service for lack of medical necessity and limits reopening to good cause or fraud or similar fault. The document should be telling readers to cite that rule.

Medical-necessity section treats InterQual, MCG and plan policies as the governing standard. Since 2024, 42 CFR 422.101(b)(6) and (c) require plans to follow Medicare statutes, regulations, NCDs and LCDs (including inpatient admission, skilled nursing, home-health and rehabilitation criteria) and allow internal criteria only where Medicare's are not fully established. This is the strongest appeal argument and it is absent.

No regulatory decision deadlines are given (72 hours expedited; 14 calendar days standard, cut to 7 calendar days from January 1, 2026 under the CMS interoperability and prior authorization rule). The 'lead times' offered instead have no source.

Claims that price-transparency machine-readable files include MA contracted rates. The payer Transparency in Coverage rule covers group and individual market plans, not Medicare Advantage; only hospital files show MA rates, and only for hospital-billed services.

Star ratings: the bonus is 5 percentage points added to the benchmark for 4 stars and above (roughly as stated), but the consequence threshold is below 3 stars sustained for three years, not '3 or fewer stars'.

Measure table errors: the annual wellness visit is not a HEDIS or Star measure; the adherence measures are Pharmacy Quality Alliance Part D measures; the HEDIS transitions measure is admission notice, discharge information, patient engagement within 30 days and medication reconciliation within 30 days, not '7/30-day follow-up'; the breast-screening age range has since been widened to start at 40. Exclusions for long-term institutional residents, institutional special-needs plan members, advanced illness with frailty and hospice are not mentioned.

The assertion that MA plans deny claims more often than other payers is backed only by a prior-authorization-request denial rate. That figure (7.7%, range 4.2% to 12.8%) matches KFF's January 2026 brief on 2024 data, not 'a 2024 KFF analysis'. The same brief's more useful findings (about one in nine denials appealed, about four in five appeals won) are left out.

Peer-to-peer is described as available after most MA medical-necessity denials within 24 to 72 hours with 30-80% reversal. Windows are plan-specific, some plans do not offer a post-decision call for MA members (the case must go to appeal), and no source is named for the reversal range.

Coordination of benefits: Medigap policies do not work with MA, so 'Medigap-equivalent products' is misleading; the ban on billing cost sharing to Qualified Medicare Beneficiaries and the handling of Medicaid as secondary to MA are missing.

'Risk adjustment does not exist in traditional Medicare fee-for-service' is overstated. HCC scores set ACO benchmarks, feed primary-care payment models and adjust MIPS cost measures, which matters to a practice that is majority fee-for-service.

Carrier profiles: Cigna sold its Medicare Advantage business to HCSC (closed March 2025) yet is profiled as a growing MA carrier; 'AARP Medicare Complete' was renamed years ago; CVS HealthHUB has been de-emphasized; the UnitedHealthcare 'CMS findings', Humana 'most generous' bonuses and 'AI looks for specific clinical language' statements are unsourced.

Compliance section says any unsupported diagnosis 'is fraudulent billing' without the False Claims Act knowledge standard, never says to correct and report unsupported codes once found, and refers to an 'annual' OIG work plan (it is updated monthly) and to unnamed OIG guidance.

Every dashboard target (5%, 2%, 90%, 6%, 80%, 85%) and the 200-patient staffing threshold is unsourced. A 'more than 90% of active conditions coded' goal assigned to a billing manager is a capture quota, the incentive design that enforcement agencies criticize.

Wellness visit: 'typically exceeds a standard E&M rate for the same time' is unsupported (the subsequent-visit code pays about the same as an established level-4 visit; verify against the current fee schedule); the once-per-calendar-year rule is a plan convention, while Original Medicare requires 11 full months between visits.
internal_contradictions: Section 1's comparison table calls the MA appeal process plan-specific, while Sections 2 and 4 describe a single CMS-mandated ladder that mirrors traditional Medicare.
Section 2 names four appeal levels; the Section 4 table has five.

Peer-to-peer timing is given as 24-72 hours, 24-48 hours and 48 hours in three places; it is to be used above a dollar threshold, yet the dashboard target is use on more than 80% of all medical-necessity denials.
The coding gap audit is annual in the fourth quarter in Section 3, quarterly on the dashboard, and run in weeks 3-4 and 9-11 of the 90-day plan regardless of the calendar.
Section 10 says the dashboard covers five domains immediately after listing six (billing operations gets no metric), and calls it monthly although cadences run from weekly to annual.

Section 3 says undercoding, not overcoding, is the costly failure; Section 8 calls risk-adjustment coding the place MA gets dangerous. A 90% capture target sits badly with the rule never to code for revenue.
Section 3 states that each diagnosis code maps to an HCC, then says not all codes carry HCC weight.
The claim that MA plans deny claims more often than other payers is supported only by a prior-authorization-request statistic.
The disclaimer says denial-rate references rest on published research, while the fact box attributes two items to unpublished vendor modeling and client data and gives no number for either.
The MA coordinator role moves from 'worth evaluating' to 'in most cases yes' to paying for itself many times over within two paragraphs and without a single figure.
time_sensitive_or_outdated: Enrollment and market-share figures are 2025 vintage (33+ million, 54%, UnitedHealthcare 29%). KFF's 2026 update shows about 35.2 million (55%), UnitedHealthcare about 26% and Humana about 20%.
Appeal dollar thresholds are 2025 amounts; 2026 amounts are $200 and $1,960, and a notice for 2027 (reportedly $200 and $2,000) is in the pipeline.
Risk-adjustment content predates V28, fully phased in for payment year 2026.
No mention that CMS excludes diagnoses from unlinked chart-review records from payment year 2027 risk scores (rate announcement of April 6, 2026), which bears directly on the chart-review warning.

No mention of the 2024 MA rule (CMS-4201-F): Medicare coverage criteria binding on plans, limits on internal criteria, authorization valid for the course of treatment, 90-day continuity for new enrollees, no retroactive medical-necessity denial after approval.

No mention of the interoperability and prior authorization rule (CMS-0057-F): 7-day standard decisions and specific denial reasons from 2026, public authorization metrics from March 2026, electronic prior-authorization interfaces due in 2027.
No mention of the 2026 MA rule (April 2025) restricting plans from reopening approved inpatient admissions.
Cigna profile is obsolete (business sold to HCSC in 2025); the 'AARP Medicare Complete' and CVS HealthHUB references are stale.
The KFF prior-authorization figure is for 2024; a later KFF analysis of 2025 data reportedly shows materially higher denial rates.
Breast-cancer screening age range (50-74) predates the NCQA change to 40-74.
The CBO projection of about 57% by 2031 sits oddly beside the 63-64% by 2034 figure quoted with it, and no report is named for either.
RADV audit expansion, the extrapolation rule and related litigation since 2023 are not covered.
'Box 23' of the CMS-1500 is paper-era framing; electronic claims carry the number in the prior-authorization reference segment.
ai_generation_signals: No author, credential, reviewer, version date or footnote anywhere; three sources are named (KFF, AMA, CBO) with no titles or links, and no regulation is cited by number in 69 pages.

Fact-box entries where the number has been deleted and replaced by a hedge ('a CCRx-modeled estimate', 'CCRx client data suggests a meaningful revenue gap'): claims of proprietary data from a product with no identifiable clients.

Hedges spliced into sentences mid-thought ('treat these as illustrative patterns rather than fixed rules', 'treat any specific percentage as directional', 'should be confirmed against current plan policy'), consistent with an automated compliance scrub.

missing_for_real_use: Any actual plan rule: no authorization lists, referral rules, portal or phone details, filing limits or dispute deadlines for any carrier, and nothing on regional plans by name.
The contracted-provider dispute path (contract clauses, provider-manual deadlines, arbitration), the non-contract path with waiver of liability, and escalation to the CMS regional office.
Regulatory citations a biller can quote in an appeal (42 CFR 422.101, 422.138, 422.566-422.634, 422.112(b)(8), 422.520).

Facility-based care: inpatient versus observation and the two-midnight benchmark, facility-held stay authorizations, concurrent review, discharge notices and fast-track appeals, skilled versus long-stay place of service, hospice election, HMO primary-care assignment and referral rules for visiting clinicians.
Special-needs plans (institutional, dual-eligible, chronic-condition), monthly election rights for institutional and dual-eligible members, and state Medicaid coordination.
Dual-eligible billing: Qualified Medicare Beneficiary protections, Medicaid crossover of MA cost sharing, bad-debt and write-off treatment.

Coverage and cost sharing for chronic care management, transitional care, advance care planning and wellness visits under each plan, including same-day visit rules.
Credentialing and enrollment with MA plans, directory attestations, NP network status.
Usable templates: appeal and reconsideration letters, a call worksheet, a contract abstract form, an authorization log, a dashboard workbook, policy language.
Metric definitions, formulas, data sources and a worked dollar example; no return-on-effort math for any recommendation.
Value-based contract mechanics: attribution, percent-of-premium math, surplus and deficit splits, stop-loss, reserves, coding-intensity adjustments.
Controls for automated or AI-assisted authorization, coding and appeal work, despite being sold alongside AI workflow material.
